page.title: Improving Golf Swing Pose Estimation
page.description: Bringing golf swing pose estimation closer to practical use through targeted dataset expansion and an efficient annotation workflow.
page.role: My role: I led annotation operations, developed the training and Core ML conversion pipeline, and collaborated with the iOS team on deployment.

sections.title: Goal
paragraphs: General-purpose pose estimation can struggle with the unusual postures and joint occlusions found in golf swings. This project aimed to improve estimation reliability in these challenging positions while keeping the model lightweight enough for real-time use on mobile devices.

sections.title: Challenges
paragraphs: We suspected that underrepresentation of golf-specific poses in the training data contributed to these failures. Expanding the dataset was our starting point, but annotation itself became a major bottleneck.

Hundreds of videos, each containing hundreds of frames, made exhaustive annotation impractical in terms of time and cost. We needed to prioritize useful footage and make labeling more efficient while maintaining consistent joint definitions.

sections.title: Contributions and Outcomes
items: Model quality: In the examples shown below, our golf-specific model produces results comparable to YOLO26x when joints are clearly visible, while handling several arm-occlusion cases more reliably. These include the follow-through in down-the-line swings and the transition in face-on swings. The model was originally developed during the YOLOv8 era.
Model efficiency: Designed for real-time inference on mobile devices, the model balances golf-specific accuracy with a lightweight architecture.
Golfer focus: The trained model can focus on the golfer while ignoring other people in the scene.
We annotated approximately 480,000 joints across 30,000 frames in about two weeks, at a cost of around US$3,000.
I worked with the team to establish objective video selection criteria, reducing the annotation workload by approximately two-thirds.
I developed practical labeling workflows and refined several joint definitions to reduce ambiguity. With my guidance, the team's labeling speed increased to approximately 3× its previous rate.
I managed an outsourced annotation team of around 10 people, coordinating the labeling work through completion.

subsections.title: Research value
paragraphs: The project offers practical insights into improving pose estimation and guiding future model development:
items: Data, not capacity: The results suggest that training data coverage was the main bottleneck in the cases studied, even with a lightweight model.
Single-frame prediction: The examples show plausible estimates under occlusion or blur without using preceding or following frames.
Lower-risk improvement: A repeatable data collection, annotation, and retraining cycle could improve accuracy without requiring a new architecture first.
Future-ready pipeline: The existing training and deployment workflow provides a foundation for integrating new models while managing research risk and cost.

subsections.title: Production engineering
paragraphs: For production, I created and delivered:
items: Cross-functional integration work with the iOS team to deploy the Core ML model in the product.
A reusable workflow for model training, inference, and Core ML conversion.
A standardized data pipeline to merge existing and newly annotated datasets for model training.

subsections.title: Reusable annotation workflow
paragraphs: I created tools and documented the workflows, joint definitions, and lessons learned so future annotation teams could build on this experience rather than solve the same problems again. The documentation covers:
items: Practical labeling techniques for faster, more consistent annotation.
The reasoning behind the joint definitions and the benefits of each choice.
Using the internal management tool to coordinate an outsourced annotation team more efficiently.
